note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Ḥiyya came to a town and asked to greet its Torah scholar, who was blind. Rabbi Ḥiyya urged Rabbi not to lower his dignity as Nasi and offered to go alone, but Rabbi took hold of him and went too. As they left, the blind scholar blessed them: you greeted one who is seen and does not see; may you greet the One Who sees and is not seen. Rabbi told Rabbi Ḥiyya he would have kept him from this blessing. Asked where he learned it, the scholar told of Rabbi Ya'akov of Ḥitiyya, who greeted his teacher daily and, when told in old age not to trouble himself, cited a verse: if seeing Sages at their death brings life, all the more so in their lifetime.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi, the Nasi; he insisted on visiting the blind scholar himself.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Traveled with Rabbi and offered to greet the blind scholar in his place.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov of the village of Ḥitiyya
people.about: Greeted his teacher every day; the blind scholar learned his blessing from his teaching.

terms.meaning: The president, the head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
An argument from the lesser to the greater: if something holds in a weaker case, all the more so in a stronger one.
